title: A Year of Holidays
bigQuestion: Why do religions keep holidays, and why do some holidays move around the calendar?

story.title: Twelve Months on One Wall
story.kicker: A class puts a sticker on the calendar for every holiday it can name, and finds a puzzle.
paragraphs: Mr. Kim hung twelve pages on the long wall, one for each month. He passed out a sheet of star stickers. "Put a star on every holiday you know," he said. "Then write its name and who keeps it."

Stars went up fast. Grace put one on December 25 for Christmas. Arjun put one in the fall for Diwali. Mei put one in late January for Lunar New Year. Daniel put one in September for Rosh Hashanah. Aisha put one in March for Eid al-Fitr.

Then Aisha frowned. "Last year Eid was in April," she said. "And when my mom was little, it was in the winter." Daniel nodded. "Rosh Hashanah moves too, but not that much." Grace said, "Christmas never moves."
Mr. Kim wrote a question on the board: Why do some holidays move? "The answer is up in the sky," he said. "Some calendars follow the sun. Some follow the moon. Some follow both."
The class looked out the window at the pale moon in the morning sky. That week, they would learn what each holiday remembers, and why its star lands where it does.
story.think: Aisha remembers Eid in March, April and winter. What might make a holiday move like that?

lessons.title: Two Clocks in the Sky
lessons.mainIdea: Some calendars count years by the sun and some count months by the moon, and a few use both.
reading: People have always watched the sky to count time. Earth goes around the sun once a year. That takes about 365 days. A calendar that follows this trip is a *solar calendar*. The calendar on most school walls is solar.

The moon changes shape as it goes around Earth. It goes from new, to full, and back to new in about 29 and a half days. That is about one month. A calendar that counts moon months is a *lunar calendar*.

Twelve moon months add up to about 354 days. That is about 11 days shorter than a sun year. Some calendars add an extra month now and then to catch up with the sun. These use both the moon and the sun.

words.d: a calendar that follows the sun; a year is about 365 days
a calendar that counts months by the moon; a year is about 354 days

look.title: Counting a Year
look.prompt: How many days shorter is a year of twelve moon months than a sun year?

check.q: What does a solar calendar follow?
check.why: Solar means of the sun. A solar year is about 365 days.

check.q: About how long is one moon month?
check.why: The moon goes from new to full and back in about 29 and a half days.

check.q: Twelve moon months are shorter than a sun year by about how much?
check.why: 365 minus 354 is 11. That gap is why lunar dates move.

lessons.title: Why Some Holidays Move
lessons.mainIdea: Holidays set by the moon move on the school calendar, while Christmas stays on one date.
reading: The Islamic calendar is *lunar*. Each year its months start about 11 days earlier on the school calendar. So Ramadan, the month of fasting, moves. Over about 33 years, it passes through every season.

Easter moves too. In many churches, Easter is the first Sunday after the first full moon of spring. So it can fall in March or April. Many Orthodox Christians use an older calendar. Their Easter is often a little later.
Christmas does not move on the school calendar. Many Christians keep it on December 25 each year. Many Orthodox Christians keep it on January 7. That date matches December 25 on their older calendar.

words.d: the Muslim month of fasting, set by the moon
the Christian holiday of Jesus's rising, set by the spring full moon

look.title: Aisha's Puzzle
look.text: Aisha says Eid was in April last year and March this year. Her mom says it was in winter when she was a girl. Grace says Christmas is always on December 25.
look.prompt: Use the words lunar and solar to explain why Eid moves and Christmas does not.

check.q: Why does Ramadan move on the school calendar?
choices: Muslims pick a new date by vote
It follows a lunar calendar that is about 11 days shorter
It is set by the spring equinox only
check.why: The Islamic calendar is lunar, so Ramadan starts about 11 days earlier each year.

check.q: How do many churches set the date of Easter?
choices: The first Sunday after the first full moon of spring
check.why: Easter depends on the spring full moon, so it moves between March and April.

check.q: Many Orthodox Christians keep Christmas on which date?
check.why: January 7 on the school calendar matches December 25 on the older calendar many Orthodox churches use.

lessons.title: Lunar New Year
lessons.mainIdea: Lunar New Year starts on a new moon in late January or February and is kept by many families in East Asia and beyond.
reading: *Lunar New Year* is a big holiday in China, Korea, Vietnam and many other places. It is set by a calendar that uses the moon and the sun. It starts on a new moon between late January and mid February.

Families clean the house to sweep out the old year. They share big meals. Children may get red envelopes with money for good luck. Many people visit older relatives and honor their *ancestors*, family members who lived long ago.
In Chicago, Chinatown holds a parade with lion and dragon dancers. The holiday is not tied to only one religion. Families of many beliefs keep it, and some keep it with no religion at all.

words.d: a new-year holiday set by a moon-and-sun calendar, kept in China, Korea, Vietnam and beyond
a family member who lived long ago, such as a great-great-grandparent

look.title: Red Envelopes
look.text: Mei's grandma hands her a red envelope. "For a good year," she says. The table has dumplings and oranges. Before eating, the family bows toward photos of Mei's great-grandparents.
look.prompt: Which two customs show hope for the new year? Which one shows honor for ancestors?

check.q: When does Lunar New Year start?
choices: On a new moon in late January or February
On the first full moon of spring
check.why: Lunar New Year begins on a new moon between late January and mid February.

check.q: What is an ancestor?
choices: A new baby in the family
A family member who lived long ago
check.why: Ancestors are family from long ago. Many families honor them at Lunar New Year.

check.q: Which is a Lunar New Year custom?
choices: Fasting from sunrise to sunset for a month
check.why: Red envelopes are a Lunar New Year custom. Colored powder belongs to Holi.

lessons.title: A New Year in the Fall
lessons.mainIdea: Rosh Hashanah is the Jewish New Year, and ten days later comes Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement.
reading: The Jewish calendar uses the moon and the sun. Its new year comes in the fall. It is called *Rosh Hashanah*. That means "head of the year" in Hebrew. People hear the *shofar*, a horn made from a ram's horn.
Many families dip apples in honey. It is a wish for a sweet new year. Rosh Hashanah is also a time to think about the past year and how to do better in the year ahead.
Ten days later comes Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement. Many Jewish adults fast for about 25 hours. They pray in the synagogue. They ask God and other people for forgiveness.

words.d: the Jewish New Year in the fall; its name means "head of the year"
a horn made from a ram's horn, blown on Rosh Hashanah
the Jewish Day of Atonement, a day of fasting and asking forgiveness

look.title: The Blowing of Trumpets
look.text: In the seventh month, in the first day of the month, shall ye have a sabbath, a memorial of blowing of trumpets, an holy convocation.
look.prompt: Jews link Rosh Hashanah to this verse. What sound does it describe?

check.q: What does Rosh Hashanah mean?
check.why: Rosh Hashanah means "head of the year"; it is the Jewish New Year.

check.q: Why do many Jewish families dip apples in honey on Rosh Hashanah?
choices: To end a month of fasting
As a wish for a sweet new year
check.why: Apples and honey stand for hope for a sweet year.

check.q: What do many Jewish adults do on Yom Kippur?
check.why: Yom Kippur is a day of fasting, prayer and asking forgiveness.

lessons.title: Passover
lessons.mainIdea: Passover remembers the story Jews tell of leaving slavery in Egypt, retold at a meal called the seder.
reading: In spring comes *Passover*. It remembers the story in the book of Exodus. Jews tell how God freed the Israelites from slavery in Egypt. Moses led them out.
Families share a special meal called a *seder*. They read the story aloud. Children ask four questions. The table has special foods. Bitter herbs remind them of the bitter times of slavery.
During Passover, many Jews eat *matzah*. It is flat bread with no yeast. The story says the Israelites left in such a hurry that their bread had no time to rise.

words.d: a Jewish spring holiday that remembers leaving slavery in Egypt
the Passover meal, where the Exodus story is read aloud
flat bread with no yeast, eaten at Passover

look.title: Keep This Day
look.text: And this day shall be unto you for a memorial; and ye shall keep it a feast to the LORD throughout your generations.
look.prompt: What does this verse ask people to do with the day? How does a seder do that?

check.q: What story does Passover remember?
choices: The Israelites leaving slavery in Egypt
check.why: Passover remembers the Exodus from Egypt, told in the Hebrew Bible.

check.q: What is matzah?
choices: A horn made from a ram
check.why: Matzah is flat bread. The story says the bread had no time to rise.

check.q: What happens at a seder?
choices: People fast all day and eat nothing
A family reads the Exodus story during a special meal
People walk seven times around the Kaaba
check.why: The seder is the Passover meal where the story is told.

lessons.title: Christmas and Easter
lessons.mainIdea: Christians celebrate Jesus's birth at Christmas and, they believe, his rising from death at Easter.
reading: *Christmas* celebrates the birth of Jesus. The story is told in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke. Christians believe Jesus is the Son of God. Many go to church, sing carols and give gifts.

*Easter* is in the spring. Christians believe Jesus died on a cross and rose from death three days later. For many Christians, Easter is the most important day of the year. Churches fill with flowers and music.
The weeks before Easter are called Lent. Many Christians give something up during Lent. They pray more or give more to others. Customs are different in Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches.

words.d: the Christian holiday celebrating the birth of Jesus
the weeks before Easter, when many Christians pray more and give things up

look.title: The Angel's News
look.text: For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord.
look.prompt: In the Gospel of Luke, an angel says this to shepherds. Which holiday retells this story?

check.q: What does Christmas celebrate?
check.why: Christmas celebrates Jesus's birth, told in Matthew and Luke.

check.q: Christians believe Easter marks what?
check.why: Christians believe Jesus rose from death, and Easter celebrates it.

check.q: What are the weeks before Easter called?
check.why: Lent is the Christian time before Easter. Ramadan is the Muslim month of fasting.

lessons.title: Ramadan and Two Eids
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims fast in daylight during Ramadan, celebrate Eid al-Fitr at its end, and keep Eid al-Adha at the time of the pilgrimage.
reading: *Ramadan* is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar. Muslims believe the Qur'an was first sent down to the Prophet Muhammad in this month. Many adult Muslims fast from dawn to sunset. At sunset, families often break the fast with dates and water.
When the new moon ends Ramadan, *Eid al-Fitr* begins. Eid means feast. Families pray together, wear new clothes and visit friends. Many give food or money to people in need.

About two months later comes Eid al-Adha. It comes at the time of the Hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca. It remembers the Qur'an's story of Abraham's obedience to God. Many families share meat with neighbors and people in need.

words.d: the Muslim feast at the end of Ramadan
the Muslim feast at the time of the Hajj, remembering Abraham
to go without food and drink for a time, often as a religious practice

look.title: The Month of Ramadan
look.text: The Qur'an was sent down in the month of Ramadan as guidance for people. Whoever is present in that month should fast.
look.prompt: According to this verse, why is Ramadan special? What practice does it name?

check.q: What do many Muslims eat first to break the fast at sunset?
check.why: Many Muslims break the Ramadan fast with dates and water.

check.q: Which holiday ends Ramadan?
check.why: Eid al-Fitr is the feast at the end of Ramadan.

check.q: Eid al-Adha comes at the time of which event?
choices: The spring full moon of Easter
The Hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca
check.why: Eid al-Adha is kept during the Hajj season.

lessons.title: Diwali and Holi
lessons.mainIdea: Diwali is the Hindu festival of lights in the fall, and Holi is the spring festival of colors.
reading: *Diwali* is the festival of lights. It comes in October or November. Families light rows of small clay lamps called diyas. Many Hindus remember the story of Prince Rama coming home. Many also pray to Lakshmi, goddess of good fortune.
Diwali lasts about five days. People clean their homes, share sweets and wear new clothes. Sikhs and Jains also keep days of light at this time, each for their own reasons.
*Holi* comes in spring, often in March. People throw bright colored powder at each other. It celebrates spring and good winning over evil. Friends and strangers laugh together, all covered in color.

words.d: the Hindu festival of lights, in October or November
the Hindu spring festival of colors
a small clay oil lamp lit at Diwali

look.title: Lamps in the Window
look.text: Arjun sets a row of diyas on the windowsill. His sister draws a colorful pattern on the floor at the door. Grandpa says, "The lights show Rama the way home."
look.prompt: What story does Grandpa's family remember? What is one thing they do to show it?

check.q: Which holiday is called the festival of lights?
check.why: Diwali is the festival of lights, with rows of diyas.

check.q: What do people throw at Holi?
choices: Flower petals only at a grave
check.why: Holi is the festival of colors.

check.q: Besides Hindus, who else keeps days of light at Diwali time?
check.why: Sikhs and Jains also keep days of light at this season, each with their own story.

lessons.title: Vesak and Vaisakhi
lessons.mainIdea: Vesak honors the Buddha on a spring full moon, and Vaisakhi is a Sikh spring holiday remembering the Khalsa.
reading: *Vesak* is a Buddhist holiday on a full moon in April or May. Many Buddhists remember the Buddha's birth, his awakening and his death on this day. They bring flowers to temples. Many light lamps and give to people in need.
Some Buddhists keep these memories on separate days. Buddhists in Japan often mark the Buddha's birth on April 8. This shows how customs differ inside one tradition.

*Vaisakhi* is kept in April, usually on April 13 or 14. It is a harvest festival in Punjab, India. For Sikhs, it remembers 1699. That year Guru Gobind Singh started the *Khalsa*, the community of committed Sikhs. Many Sikhs march in parades and share free meals.

words.d: a Buddhist holiday on a spring full moon honoring the Buddha
a Sikh and Punjabi spring holiday in April
the community of committed Sikhs, begun by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699

look.title: Two Parades in Spring
look.text: In April, Sikh families march with music and flags and serve free food to anyone who comes. In May, a Buddhist temple fills with flowers and lamps. A child pours water over a small statue of the baby Buddha.
look.prompt: Which scene is Vaisakhi and which is Vesak? What clue told you?

check.q: Which holiday honors the Buddha on a spring full moon?
check.why: Vesak honors the Buddha's birth, awakening and death on a full moon.

check.q: What does Vaisakhi remember for Sikhs?
choices: The start of the Khalsa in 1699
check.why: Guru Gobind Singh started the Khalsa at Vaisakhi in 1699.

check.q: Who started the Khalsa?
check.why: Guru Gobind Singh was the tenth Sikh Guru.

lessons.title: A Year on One Wall
lessons.mainIdea: Putting holidays on one calendar shows what each one remembers and how different calendars work together.
reading: Look at a full year of holidays. Each one *commemorates* something. That means it remembers an event or honors a person. Passover remembers the Exodus. Christmas remembers Jesus's birth. Vesak remembers the Buddha.
Some holidays last one day. Others last about a week or even more. Ramadan lasts a whole month. The length is one way a tradition shows what matters most to it.
A shared calendar helps a school be fair. Teachers can plan tests so they do not land on big holidays. Friends can learn when to say "Happy Diwali" or "Eid Mubarak."

words.d: to remember an event or honor a person with a special day
a chart of the days, weeks and months of a year

look.title: How Long Some Holidays Last
look.cite: Common calendar facts; lengths vary by place and community
look.prompt: Which lasts the longest? Which lasts about a week?

check.q: What does commemorate mean?
choices: To fast from dawn to sunset
To move a holiday to a new date
To remember an event or honor a person with a special day
check.why: To commemorate is to remember. Most holidays commemorate something.

check.q: Which holiday lasts about a whole month?
check.why: Ramadan is a month of fasting, 29 or 30 days.

check.q: How can a shared calendar help a school?
choices: Teachers can plan tests so they avoid big holidays
It tells students which religion to join
It makes every holiday the same day
check.why: Knowing the holidays helps a school be fair to every family.

review.q: Why do Ramadan and Eid move on the school calendar?
choices: The Islamic calendar follows the sun
The Islamic calendar follows the moon
Families choose a new date each year
They always come right after Christmas
review.why: The lunar year is about 11 days shorter, so the dates move earlier each year.

review.q: Which holiday stays on the same date each year for most Christians?
review.why: Many Christians keep Christmas on December 25. Easter follows the spring moon.

review.q: Which holiday remembers leaving slavery in Egypt?
review.why: Passover retells the Exodus at the seder.
Diwali is the festival of lights. The other pairs mix up the customs.

review.q: A Sikh family marches in an April parade and serves free food. Which holiday is it?
review.why: Vaisakhi is the Sikh spring holiday remembering the Khalsa.

choices: A clay lamp lit at Diwali
A horn blown on Rosh Hashanah
review.why: The shofar is made from a ram's horn.

review.q: Which holiday is kept by families of many beliefs in China, Korea and Vietnam?
review.why: Lunar New Year is not tied to one religion.
Vesak remembers the Buddha's birth, awakening and death.
